metadata.title: Exploring the predictors of teachers’ teaching autonomy: A three-level international study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 (OECD) three-level nested data (teachers within schools within countries/regions) and applies a multilevel modeling strategy (HLM) to account for clustering. The methodology describes TALIS’s two-stage systematic sampling with probability proportional to size within categories and random teacher selection within schools, but it does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme. Because the analysis is not ML-based and instead uses hierarchical linear modeling in Mplus, the manuscript does not specify a weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT-style identifiers) and therefore weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Analysts should, in principle, use TALIS-provided sampling weights when estimating population-representative effects; however, this paper’s results are best interpreted as model-based associations under the reported multilevel structure rather than explicitly weight-adjusted estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data come from TALIS 2018 third wave for lower secondary education (ISCED 2) in 48 countries/regions. The analytic sample includes 118,347 teachers from 8,262 schools in 27 countries after excluding cases with missing values for variables included in the study. The paper does not provide per-country teacher counts in the provided text, so country-level n cannot be extracted here; the analysis is restricted to teachers/principals in lower secondary schools and to the specific questionnaire items used to construct the teaching autonomy outcome and the predictor scales/indices.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Wave 3) Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — teachers’ teaching autonomy (4-point Likert, 5 items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level HLM (Mplus 8.3). Null model variance decomposition: ICC teacher 82.70%, school 10.43%, country 6.87%. Full conditional model (Model 9) total R2: 9.41% (teacher 8.92%, school 14.63%, country 7.41%). Significant standardized coefficients include: Self-efficacy β=0.174 (p<0.001), Instructional quality β=0.058 (p<0.001), Professional preparedness β=0.060 (p<0.001), Permanent contract β=0.016 (p<0.05), Individual vs collaboration time β=0.114 (p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Wave 3) lower secondary (ISCED 2) the study leveraged self-efficacy, instructional quality, professional preparedness, permanent contract status, and teachers’ individual vs collaboration time allocation to model teachers’ teaching autonomy, finding that professionalism and individualism-related predictors were the strongest positive associations while most complexity predictors were not significant. This indicates that policy and school leadership efforts should prioritize teacher professional development, instructional capability, and autonomy-supportive governance (e.g., distributed leadership and enabling individual work preferences), rather than expecting class-composition complexity alone to drive autonomy.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 (Wave 3) data for lower secondary education (ISCED 2) across 27 countries/regions, using a three-level hierarchical linear model (teachers within schools within countries). The dependent variable is teachers’ teaching autonomy measured on a 4-point Likert scale from five items (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.826). After excluding cases with missing values for included variables, the analytic sample comprises 118,347 teachers from 8,262 schools. In the null model, 82.7% of variance is at the teacher level, 10.43% at the school level, and 6.87% at the country level; in the full conditional model, total R2 reaches 9.41%. The strongest positive associations come from professionalism and culture of individualism mechanisms (e.g., self-efficacy β≈0.174, instructional quality β≈0.058, individual vs collaboration time ratio β≈0.114), while complexity-of-practice indicators are mostly non-significant. Limitations include cross-sectional TALIS timing, and the manuscript does not report explicit sampling-weight usage in the provided text.
